paragraphs.simple: A magic tree house full of books appeared in the Frog Creek woods. It takes Jack and Annie to any time and place in history.

background.note: The made-up town where Jack and Annie live, in the US state of Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.simple: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay. Jack and Annie have done many jobs for Morgan and Merlin. Teddy and Kathleen sometimes help them.

background.note: The castle and town of King Arthur in old English stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: Now Teddy and Kathleen are in urgent need of Jack and Annie’s help.
paragraphs.simple: Teddy made a mistake with magic and turned Merlin's penguin, Penny, into a statue. He is afraid he will be sent away from Camelot.

paragraphs.context: Teddy and Kathleen have found an ancient spell that will undo Teddy
paragraphs.simple: To undo the spell, Jack and Annie must find four special things from different times and places. They have found three. Now they need the last one.

paragraphs.simple: Jack dreams that Teddy and Kathleen are knocking. He wants to help them, but his legs will not move.

paragraphs.simple: Jack opens his eyes. At first he does not know where he is.

paragraphs.simple: Dad tells Jack to get up for school.

paragraphs.context: What a dream, thought Jack. He quickly sat up in bed. He’d overslept!
paragraphs.simple: It was only a dream. Jack sits up fast. He slept too long!

paragraphs.simple: Dad looks into the room and asks if Jack is awake.

paragraphs.simple: Dad tells Jack to hurry and closes the door.

paragraphs.simple: Jack jumps out of bed. They wanted to go to the tree house before school. Today they must find the fourth thing to save Penny.

paragraphs.context: Jack pulled on his jeans and a T-shirt and rushed out
paragraphs.simple: Jack dresses fast and runs out. Annie runs out at the same time. They both slept too long.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must get to the tree house before school starts.

paragraphs.simple: They run down the stairs into the kitchen.

paragraphs.context: “Good morning, sleepyheads,” their mom said.
paragraphs.simple: Mom made egg sandwiches. There is just enough time for breakfast.

paragraphs.simple: Jack asks to take the sandwiches with them. He says they must go to school early for a special project. (It is really their mission.)

paragraphs.context: “You guys really seem to love school,” their dad said.
paragraphs.simple: Dad says they really seem to love school.

paragraphs.context: “Yep, school’s great,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says school is great. (He wants to go to the tree house.)

paragraphs.simple: They go out of the front door. The spring air is a little wet.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says they have twenty-five minutes before school.

paragraphs.simple: They climb the rope ladder into the tree house and sit down to rest and breathe.

paragraphs.simple: After the earthquake, many people heard about the pandas and wanted to help them.

paragraphs.context: Many organizations were already working hard to save pandas from extinction—groups
paragraphs.simple: Many groups work to save pandas. Now pandas are a symbol for protecting all animals that are in danger.

background.note: A big international group that works to protect nature. Its sign is a panda.

paragraphs.context: The panda’s roly-poly body and innocent, shy eyes evoke feelings
paragraphs.simple: Pandas' round bodies and shy eyes make people feel wonder and love. Pandas bring out the best in people. That is one good reason to keep them alive.

sentences.context: While Merlin and Morgan were away from Camelot, Teddy accidentally put a spell on Penny, Merlin’s beloved penguin, turning her into a statue.
sentences.simple: When Merlin and Morgan were not in Camelot, Teddy put a spell on Merlin's dear penguin Penny by mistake, and she became a statue.
sentences.main: Teddy accidentally put a spell on Penny.

parts.text: While Merlin and Morgan were away from Camelot,
parts.meaning: When Merlin and Morgan were not in Camelot,

parts.text: Teddy accidentally put a spell on Penny,
parts.meaning: Teddy put a spell on Penny by mistake,

parts.text: Merlin’s beloved penguin,
parts.meaning: the penguin that Merlin loves,

parts.text: turning her into a statue.
parts.meaning: and so she became a statue.

sentences.grammar: "While" + past tense tells what was happening at that time. "Turning her into ..." (-ing) tells the result of the action.

sentences.context: We haven’t yet finished translating the last lines of the secret rhyme to reverse the statue spell Teddy cast on Penny.
sentences.simple: We have not finished changing the last lines of the secret rhyme into our language. The rhyme can undo the spell that Teddy put on Penny.
sentences.main: We haven't finished translating the rhyme.

parts.text: We haven’t yet finished translating
parts.meaning: We have still not finished putting into our language

parts.text: the last lines of the secret rhyme
parts.meaning: the last lines of the secret poem

parts.text: to reverse the statue spell
parts.job: What the rhyme is for ("to" = in order to).
parts.meaning: that can undo the spell that made a statue

parts.text: Teddy cast on Penny.
parts.meaning: that Teddy put on Penny.

sentences.grammar: "Haven't yet" = not until now. "The spell Teddy cast" = "the spell that Teddy cast"; "that" can be left out.

sentences.context: The tree house was in the tallest tree in a grove at the edge of a quiet street.
sentences.simple: The tree house was in the highest tree of a small group of trees, next to a quiet street.
sentences.main: The tree house was in the tallest tree.

parts.text: The tree house was in the tallest tree
parts.job: Main idea: where the tree house was.
parts.meaning: The tree house was in the highest tree

parts.text: in a grove
parts.meaning: in a small group of trees

parts.text: at the edge of a quiet street.
parts.meaning: beside a quiet street.

sentences.grammar: "The tallest" = more tall than all the others (superlative). Place phrases ("in ...", "at ...") follow one after another.

sentences.context: Wolong Town is inside the Wolong National Nature Reserve, which is circled by a mountain range called the Sleeping Dragon.
sentences.simple: Wolong Town is in the Wolong National Nature Reserve. A line of mountains called the Sleeping Dragon goes around the reserve.
sentences.main: Wolong Town is inside the reserve.

parts.text: Wolong Town is inside the Wolong National Nature Reserve,
parts.job: Main idea: where the town is.
parts.meaning: Wolong Town is in the Wolong nature reserve,

parts.text: which is circled by a mountain range
parts.job: More about the reserve (passive: "is circled by").
parts.meaning: and a line of mountains goes all around it

parts.text: called the Sleeping Dragon.
parts.meaning: with the name the Sleeping Dragon.

sentences.grammar: ", which ..." adds information about the thing just named. "Is circled by" (passive) = the mountains circle it.

sentences.context: How could he have let Annie talk him into riding bikes on a highway?
sentences.simple: Why did he let Annie make him agree to ride bikes on a big, busy road? It was a bad idea.
sentences.main: He should not have let Annie talk him into it.

parts.text: How could he have let Annie
parts.job: Main idea: Jack is angry with himself ("could have" + past participle).
parts.meaning: Why did he let Annie

parts.text: talk him into riding bikes on a highway?
parts.job: What Annie made him do ("talk someone into" + -ing).
parts.meaning: make him agree to ride bikes on a big road?

sentences.grammar: "How could he have ...?" shows he is sorry about something he did. "Talk someone into doing" = make them agree to do it.

sentences.context: Now those same forests are being cut down to make room for farms and roads.
sentences.simple: Now people are cutting down those forests so they can have space for farms and roads.
sentences.main: The forests are being cut down.

parts.text: Now those same forests are being cut down
parts.meaning: Now people are cutting down those forests

parts.text: to make room for farms and roads.
parts.meaning: so there is space for farms and roads.

sentences.grammar: "Are being cut" = present continuous passive: it is happening now, and we do not say who does it. "Make room for" = make space for.

sentences.context: He felt as if he and Annie were zoo animals and the panda was a curious visitor observing them.
sentences.simple: He felt like he and Annie were animals in a zoo, and the panda was a visitor who wanted to know about them and was watching them.
sentences.main: He felt like a zoo animal.

parts.text: He felt as if
parts.job: Main idea: how Jack felt ("as if" + past).
parts.meaning: He felt like

parts.text: he and Annie were zoo animals
parts.job: The first part of the picture in his mind.
parts.meaning: he and Annie were animals in a zoo

parts.text: and the panda was a curious visitor observing them.
parts.job: The second part ("observing" = who was watching).
parts.meaning: and the panda was a visitor watching them with interest.

sentences.grammar: "As if" + past tense ("were") tells how something seemed, not how it really was.

sentences.context: He didn’t know what to write—words couldn’t possibly capture the wonder of her.
sentences.simple: He did not know what to write, because words could never show how wonderful she was.
sentences.main: Words couldn't capture the wonder of her.

parts.text: He didn’t know what to write
parts.meaning: He did not know what he should write

parts.text: —words couldn’t possibly capture the wonder of her.
parts.meaning: because no words could show how wonderful she was.

sentences.grammar: "What to write" = what he should write. "Couldn't possibly" = could not in any way. "Capture" here = show in words.

sentences.context: No sooner had Jack said that than another enormous boulder crashed to the ground.
sentences.simple: Just as Jack said that, another very big rock crashed to the ground.
sentences.main: Right after Jack spoke, another boulder crashed down.

parts.text: No sooner had Jack said that
parts.meaning: Just as Jack finished saying that

parts.text: than another enormous boulder crashed to the ground.
parts.meaning: another very big rock crashed down.

sentences.grammar: "No sooner had ... than ..." = the second thing happened right after the first. Note the word order "had Jack said".

sentences.context: A boulder the size of a car had crushed both their bikes.
sentences.simple: A rock as big as a car had fallen on their bikes and broken them.
sentences.main: A boulder had crushed their bikes.

parts.text: A boulder the size of a car
parts.job: Who (the subject) and how big it was.
parts.meaning: A rock as big as a car

parts.text: had crushed both their bikes.
parts.job: Main idea (past perfect: it happened before they looked).
parts.meaning: had broken both of their bikes.

sentences.grammar: "The size of a car" = as big as a car. "Had crushed" (past perfect) = it happened before the moment in the story.

sentences.context: He leapt over a river of water coursing down from the mountain as if it were a rain puddle.
sentences.simple: He jumped over a river of water running fast down the mountain, as easily as if it were a small puddle.
sentences.main: He leapt over a river like a puddle.

parts.text: He leapt over a river of water
parts.meaning: He jumped over a river of water

parts.text: coursing down from the mountain
parts.meaning: that was running fast down the mountain

parts.text: as if it were a rain puddle.
parts.job: How easy it was ("as if" + were).
parts.meaning: as easily as jumping over a small pool of rain.

sentences.grammar: "Leapt" is a past form of "leap". "As if it were" = like it was (it was not really).

sentences.context: He figured the last thing the staff needed now was to see a twenty-five-foot-tall kid.
sentences.simple: He thought the workers really did not need to see a giant kid now.
sentences.main: The staff did not need to see a giant kid.

parts.text: He figured
parts.job: Main idea: what Jack thought ("figure" = think).
parts.meaning: He thought

parts.text: the last thing the staff needed now
parts.job: The subject of the next part ("the last thing" = what they need least).
parts.meaning: what the workers needed least of all now

parts.text: was to see a twenty-five-foot-tall kid.
parts.meaning: was to see a kid as tall as a house.

sentences.grammar: "The last thing someone needs" = something they do not want at all. "Twenty-five-foot-tall" is one long adjective with hyphens.

sentences.context: And people speak up for them because they can’t speak up for themselves.
sentences.simple: And people talk for the pandas, because the pandas cannot talk for themselves.

parts.text: And people speak up for them
parts.job: Main idea ("speak up for" = speak to help someone).
parts.meaning: And people say things to help the pandas

parts.text: because they can’t speak up for themselves.
parts.meaning: because the pandas cannot do it for themselves.

sentences.grammar: "Speak up for" someone = say things to help or protect them. "Themselves" points back to "they" (the pandas).

sentences.context: They only served to awaken feelings deep within you, Teddy.
sentences.simple: They only helped to wake up the feelings that were deep inside you, Teddy.

parts.text: They only served
parts.job: Main idea ("serve to" = be used to, help to).
parts.meaning: They only helped

parts.text: to awaken feelings deep within you, Teddy.
parts.meaning: to wake up the feelings deep inside you, Teddy.

sentences.grammar: "Served to" + verb = had the result of. "Deep within you" = deep inside you.

sentences.context: Pandas seem to bring out the best in people.
sentences.simple: Pandas seem to make people show their best and kindest side.
sentences.main: Pandas bring out the best in people.

parts.text: Pandas seem to
parts.meaning: It looks like pandas

parts.text: bring out the best in people.
parts.job: What pandas do ("bring out" = make it show).
parts.meaning: make people show the best part of themselves.

sentences.grammar: "Seem to" + verb = it looks true. "Bring out the best in someone" = make them act in their best way.

back up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

belong to.meaning: If a thing belongs to you, it is yours.

belong to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

bend down.meaning: To move the top of your body down toward the ground.

bend down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break of day.meaning: Dawn; the time when the sun comes up.
break of day.example: Morgan and Merlin will return by break of day tomorrow!

break off.meaning: (Of a piece) to break and come away.
break off.example: Jack struggled to break off a piece.
break off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break the silence.meaning: To be the first to speak after a quiet time.
break the silence.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break the spell.meaning: To end a magic spell, so things become normal again.
break the spell.example: But we do know the fourth object we need to break the spell.
break the spell.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring forth.meaning: (Old way to say it.) To bring something out and show it.
bring forth.example: “Bring forth the four things you found to break the spell,” said Teddy.
bring forth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring out.meaning: To help something hidden inside someone to show itself ("bring out Barry's instincts").
bring out.example: Pandas seem to bring out the best in people.
bring out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

burst into laughter.meaning: To suddenly start to laugh loudly.
burst into laughter.example: they said together, and then they burst into laughter.
burst into laughter.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by mistake.meaning: Not on purpose; because of an error.
by mistake.example: She might be so upset and confused that she could attack you by mistake.”
by mistake.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

by the time.meaning: "By the time they reached the tree" means at the moment when they reached it (and not before).
by the time.example: By the time he entered the bike shop, she was already talking with the man who worked there.
by the time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

call out.meaning: To shout something so that people can hear, for example to sell things.
call out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

can't help.meaning: "He couldn't help crying out" = he could not stop himself from crying out.
can't help.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

can't wait.meaning: To be very excited and want something to happen very soon.
can't wait.example: Suddenly he couldn’t wait to be there and help bring Penny back to life.
can't wait.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch sight of.meaning: To suddenly see someone or something.
catch sight of.example: Ling caught sight of Jack and Annie, they both stopped dead in their tracks and gaped at them.
catch sight of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

catch your breath.meaning: To rest until you can breathe normally again.
catch your breath.example: Inside the tree house they both sat on the floor, catching their breath.
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cell phone.meaning: A mobile phone. (In 1970, there were none.)
cell phone.example: “Yes, I received a call on my cell phone from the military,” said Dr.
cell phone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

check on.meaning: To go and see if something is all right.
check on.example: Then he gave Jack and Annie menus and went to check on other customers.
check on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

climb on.meaning: To get onto something, like a sled or a horse.
climb on.example: Jack and Annie were both laughing as they climbed on their mountain bikes and started back toward Wolong Town.
climb on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come alive.meaning: To start living; (of a statue) to become a living thing.
come alive.example: She looked like a gigantic stuffed animal that had come alive.
come alive.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come along.meaning: "Come along" = come with me; hurry up.
come along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come back to life.meaning: To start moving or living again.
come back to life.example: We hoped that she might come back to life in Merlin’s favorite place.
come back to life.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come on.meaning: "Come on!" means "Hurry!", "Let's go!" or "Please do it!"
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come out.meaning: To go outside, or come out of a place where you were hidden.
come out.example: The sun had come out from behind the clouds.
come out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come true.meaning: When a dream or a wish comes true, it really happens.
come true.example: “My life’s dream has finally come true!”
come true.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

crash down.example: A huge boulder crashed down the mountain slope beside them.
crash down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

crazy about.meaning: Liking or loving someone or something very much.
crazy about.example: Why are you acting so crazy about pandas?”
crazy about.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cut down.meaning: To cut a tree so that it falls to the ground.
cut down.example: Now those same forests are being cut down to make room for farms and roads.”
cut down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do the right thing.meaning: To do what is good and fair.
do the right thing.example: “Remember on our last mission, you said that when we do the right thing, it feels like it somehow helps Penny—even if it seems to take us away from our goal?”
do the right thing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do you mind.meaning: A polite way to ask for something. "Do you mind taking us...?" means "Can you please take us...?"
do you mind.example: Do you mind if we tag along with you, Sylvia?”
do you mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

even if.meaning: It does not matter if this happens; the result is the same.
even if.example: “Remember on our last mission, you said that when we do the right thing, it feels like it somehow helps Penny—even if it seems to take us away from our goal?”
even if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fall in love with.meaning: To start to love someone or something.
fall in love with.example: According to legend, a dragon fell in love with the beauty of the mountains and trees.
fall in love with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

faster and faster.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

feel sorry for.meaning: To feel sad for someone who has a problem.
feel sorry for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it or find the answer.
figure out.example: As Jack tried to figure out what to do, another boulder tumbled down—and then another!
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.example: They have found three of these objects—and now they are waiting to find out where they must go next, and what they must find….
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find your way.meaning: To find the right way to a place.
find your way.example: We helped a funny dog find out that he was a great dog, and a president find hope, and some pandas find their way home.”
find your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

first aid.meaning: Quick help for someone who is hurt, before a doctor comes. A "first-aid kit" is a box of things for this.
first aid.example: Staff members were rushing around with buckets, shovels, and first-aid kits.
first aid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly.
flip through.example: She took the guide book and flipped through the pages until she found photos of pandas.
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for a moment.example: For a moment, the panda wasn’t eight years old.
for a moment.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for nothing.meaning: "They don't call him the Master of Escape for nothing" = there is a good reason for that name.
for nothing.example: “We came all this way for nothing?”
for nothing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for once.meaning: This one time (it does not usually happen).
for once.example: “And look—we get to wear our own clothes for once.”
for once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fresh air.example: Jack and Annie didn’t move for a moment, breathing in the clean, fresh air.
fresh air.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

from memory.meaning: Without looking at the words, because you have learned them.
from memory.example: “Yes, I do,” said Teddy. Then he recited the words from memory:
from memory.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

from side to side.meaning: Moving to the left and then to the right, again and again.
from side to side.example: He saw Master Lee dancing with Bing-Bing, holding her paws and rocking from side to side.
from side to side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

gather up.meaning: To pick up and collect things that are spread out.
gather up.example: Jack gathered up the jewel, the flower, the feather, and the panda bread.
gather up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get away from.meaning: To leave a person or place quickly, to be safe.
get away from.example: “Lots more,” said Jack, “especially if we have to get away from cobras again.”
get away from.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get back.example: Now they could get back to their mission.
get back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get by.meaning: To manage to live or do things with very little.
get by.example: “We will set up tents and carry water from the stream and get by as best we can,” said Dr.
get by.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get in trouble.meaning: To be punished or have problems because you did something wrong.
get in trouble.example: “Let’s grab our bikes and go—before Sylvia gets in trouble.”
get in trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get out of.example: “It’s the only way we can get out of here.”
get out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get over.meaning: To climb or go over something ("get over this stuff").
get over.example: “You’d have to be King Kong to get over this stuff.”
get over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get to work.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

good day.example: “You two have a good day,” she said.
good day.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

good for.meaning: "Good for her!" = I am glad she did that; well done.
good for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

good grief.meaning: "Good grief!" is a sound you make when you are surprised or a little annoyed.
good grief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

good luck.meaning: I hope things go well for you.
good luck.example: “Good luck rebuilding the panda center,” said Jack.
good luck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

grown ups.meaning: (Written "grown-ups"; one is a "grown-up".) Adults; people who are not children any more.
grown ups.example: Near the gate a group of grown-ups was waiting to go inside.
grown ups.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

had better.meaning: "We'd better go" means we should go, or something bad may happen.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

have fun.example: “But we’ll have fun looking for it.
have fun.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have no choice but to.meaning: To have to do something, because there is no other way.
have no choice but to.example: He had no choice but to follow Annie into the panda center.
have no choice but to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

head back.example: Then he turned and headed back to Bing-Bing’s house.
head back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

help out.meaning: To help someone, especially when they are busy or have problems.
help out.example: It’s nice to help out here.”
help out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold on.meaning: 1. To hold something firmly ("held on tightly"). 2. "Hold on!" = Wait a moment!
hold on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold up.meaning: To lift something and hold it high, so people can see it.
hold up.example: Jack held up his hand, interrupting her.
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or excited.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

hot dog.meaning: A long sausage in a long, soft bread roll.
hot dog.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

how about.meaning: "How about ...?" = What do you think of ...? Let's have ...!
how about.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

huff and puff.example: As they struggled uphill, huffing and puffing, a light rain started to fall.
huff and puff.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i get it.example: “Oh, now I get it,” said Annie.
i get it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

i guess.meaning: "I guess" means "I think so, but I am not sure."

i'm afraid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in a daze.meaning: Not able to think clearly, as if half asleep.

in a daze.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in an instant.example: In an instant he had shrunk back to his normal size.
in an instant.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
